Prevention: Use resistant crop varieties, contact local extension officer for advice on locally available varieties.
Plant nurseries away from areas of known infestation.
Apply mulch to improve health of crops and reduce impact from potential infestations.
Plant perennial hedges (e.g. pigeon pea) to attract predatory mites to kill
Actively remove weeds form plantations to reduce suitable habitat for mite infestations.
Undertale suitable phytosanitary practices, wash clothing and tools used in infested areas before entering new ones.
Avoid the use of broad spectrum insecticides to conserve natural predators such as predatory mites, spiders, lacewings, and ladybird beetles.
Monitoring: Actively monitor crops for mite activity, note that it may be hard to distinguish between mite infestation symptoms and nutrient deficiency.
If so, observe 10 random leaves per 20 plants for small red mites.
Mite colonies are commonly found on the supper surface of old leaves, but may move to either surface of young leaves under drought conditions and heavy infestations.
Mites are around 360µm long, with dark red, oval bodies.
Males may appear to have a slightly elongated dorsal end.
Symptoms of infestation include yellow spots on leaves, turning brown and necrotic under heavy infestations.
Defoliation may occur in heavily infested plants.
When mites are identified or symptoms first appear, consider undertaking direct control actions.
Direct Control: Remove infested plant parts and destroy by burning.
Use of a soap spray (3 tablespoons of liquid soap with 4 litres of water).
Apply during the early morning or late afternoon.
Use of neem seed kernel extract spray (grind 500 g of neem seed kernels and mix with 10 litres of water).
Spray during dry periods as rainfall will wash off the solution.
Use of flour solution spray (2 cups of flour with 5-10 litres of water).
Apply to the underside of leaves, when the solution dries during the day any mites present will be encrusted in flour and die.
